query: For refractory materials, experiments at the solid-to-fluid transition are difficult and yield sparse, scattered data, while the large compositional space of high-entropy systems makes systematic screening impractical. DFT free-energy studies can determine the transition from the crossing of solid and dense-fluid Gibbs energies and provide associated thermodynamic properties, but their reliance on extensive ab initio molecular dynamics makes them costly. TOR-TILD has shown high efficiency for elemental and binary systems, yet becomes substantially slower for multicomponent systems. Any broadly useful approach must retain ab initio-level accuracy, represent all thermodynamic effects identified as important, treat both phases around the transition, and remain practical across relevant compositions and temperatures. For a multicomponent high-entropy material in these high-temperature states, what single intervention could improve determination of transition temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change, and dense-fluid heat capacity? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and causal mechanism, its predicted outcome relative to existing experimental and computational baselines, its boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive experiment or benchmark that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The incorporation of deep learning potentials in simulations of high-entropy materials can improve the determination of transition temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change, and dense-fluid heat capacity.
generation.intervention: Incorporation of deep learning potentials in simulations
generation.mechanism: Enhanced prediction accuracy through deep learning potentials, improved representation of thermodynamic effects
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved determination of transition temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change, and dense-fluid heat capacity, with increased accuracy and efficiency compared to existing computational methods
generation.baseline: Existing computational methods, such as DFT and CALPHAD
generation.boundary: Applicability limited to high-entropy materials, computational resources and training data requirements
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty in the accuracy of deep learning potentials for high-entropy materials, potential limitations in representing complex thermodynamic effects

falsification_experiment.design: Comparison of simulation results using deep learning potentials and existing computational methods for a range of high-entropy materials and compositions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the deep learning potential simulations do not show improved accuracy and efficiency compared to existing computational methods, the hypothesis is falsified

Melting simulations of high-entropy carbonitrides by deep learning potentials

Abstract: The melting temperature is a crucial property of materials that determines their potential applications in different industrial fields. In this study, we used a deep neural network potential to describe the structure of high-entropy (TiZrTaHfNb)CxN1−x carbonitrides (HECN) in both solid and liquid states. This approach allows us to predict heating and cooling temperatures depending on the nitrogen content to determine the melting temperature and analyze structure changes from atomistic point of view. A steady increase in nitrogen content leads to increasing melting temperature, with a maximum approaching for 25% of nitrogen in the HECN. A careful analysis of pair correlations, together with calculations of entropy in the considered liquid phases of HECNs allows us to explain the origin of the nonlinear enhancement of the melting temperature with increasing nitrogen content. The maximum melting temperature of 3580 ± 30 K belongs to (TiZrTaHfNb)C0.75N0.25 composition.
